    Content from EIC France 2026 ePIC Tutorial Introduction

    Last updated on 2026-11-06 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 30 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What will we be doing in this tutorial?
    • What is eic-shell?
    • What is in the EIC software stack?

    Objectives

    • Explore the EIC software stack

    Introduction

    In this tutorial we will explore some key components and use cases of the ePIC software stack. We will take the files generated in the previous tutorial and process them through the simulation of the ePIC detector. We will then reconstruct the output of the simulation. Finally, we will then analyse the output of this reconstruction and try to identify events of interest.

    This is analogous to a real experiment:

    • Real experiment
      • Collisions \(\rightarrow\) Raw signals in detector \(\rightarrow\) Reconstruct raw signals \(\rightarrow\) Analyse reconstructed output
    • Simulation
      • Generate events of interest \(\rightarrow\) Raw energy depositions in simulation \(\rightarrow\) Reconstruct raw signals \(\rightarrow\) Analyse reconstructed output

    This analogy is intentional. We’re a little way away from “real” ePIC data, so simulations are all we have from now. However, we don’t want to develop a framework that’s only useful for simulations! We should analyse our simulations in the same way that we intend to organise and analyse real data. This should smooth the transition to actual running and ensure that we have people (you!) trained on how to analyse and interpret experimental data from day one.

    Introduction - eic-shell

    eic-shell is the environment in which we will be running our simulation and reconstruction. This container comes with a range of pre-compiled software. The versions of software installed in a given container version are known and maintained. This is for reproducibility purposes. If you run a simulation in eic-shell and see an issue, you can quote the version of the container you’re using when reporting the issue. This helps narrow down issues rapidly.

    When you run

    BASH 

    ./eic-shell

    you should load into the container. If you have loaded the container successfully you should see jug_dev> $User@$Host in your terminal.

    Callout

    Escaping eic-shell

    To leave the eic-shell environment, just type:

    BASH 

    exit

    into your terminal.

    Within eic-shell, you can use the command

    BASH 

    eic-info

    to check the versions of lots of software. This will provide a large info dump, you can narrow it down via grep commands. For example, you can check your container versions via:

    BASH 

    eic-info | grep jug_dev

    to get the specific container image you’re using.

    Introduction - The ePIC Software Stack

    In simulating and reconstructing EIC/ePIC data, a large range of different software packages are used. Where possible, applicable software from other HEP experiments is utilised. For example ACTS is used for tracking.

    A clickable version is available on the eic.github.io page. Much of this software is pre-installed in eic-shell.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Check a piece of the software stack

    Within eic-shell, pick a piece of the ePIC software stack from the diagram above and check what version is in use in the container you’ve just loaded.

    Callout

    Switching Container Version

    By default, when we load the container via CVFMS (or update it), we will get the latest nightly release. There are specific reasons you may wash to load a different container version though. To install a specific version, you can run:

    BASH 

    ./install.sh -v <<version>>

    when you execute your install command. As an example 26.07.0-stable is the July 2026 (version 0) container.

    If you are running on a system with CVFMS (e.g. JLab or BNL farms), you can just run:

    BASH 

    ./eic-shell --version <<version>>

    to switch to your desired container version.

    Key Points
    • The ePIC software stack will be used to simulate and reconstruct our generated events
    • The intention is that this stack is as comparable to the “final” experimental software as possible
    • eic-shell contains pre-compiled versions of a whole host of software
    • Keep careful track of the container you’re using

    Content from Simulating ePIC Events

    Last updated on 2026-11-06 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 30 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can we use the simulation of the ePIC detector?
    • What geometries are available?

    Objectives

    • Process our event generator sample through the ePIC detector simulation

    Introduction

    The ePIC simulation is pre-installed within eic-shell. The ePIC geometry is defined in the DD4HEP (Detector Description for High Energy Physics) framework. More info can be found in the tutorials on DD4HEP to define ePIC detectors and Using npsim and Geant4

    Crucially, DD4HEP acts as a wrapper around the familiar Geant4 Monte-Carlo simulation toolkit.

    Introduction - Setup

    To run a simulation, we need to enter eic-shell if we’re not already there:

    BASH 

    ./eic-shell

    Once inside, we need to load in a geometry. We can choose different options of we want, but we will use epic-main:

    BASH 

    source /opt/detector/epic-main/bin/thisepic.sh
    Callout

    Other Geometries

    You can do

    BASH 

    ls -lrth /opt/detector/

    to view the other versions of the detector geometry available in eic-shell. These are tagged by month typically. They should have a corresponding thisepic.sh script you could source instead in their /bin/ directory.

    Before we run anything, we’ll make a directory to run in to keep things neat:

    BASH 

    mkdir EIC_France_Simulations && cd EIC_France_Simulations

    Copy your generated event file from earlier into this directory too. We’re now ready to simulate!

    Running Simulations

    We will run our simulation using the npsim command.

    Callout

    npsim vs ddsim

    In other tutorials, you may see reference to ddsim as well as npsim? Is this the same thing?

    Not quite. They are very similar, but npsim effectively runs with a set of extra flags. Crucially, these flags enable the simulation of optical photons. As such, npsim should be used whenever optical photons are important for your output - e.g. in calorimetry or Cherenkov detectors. For rapid simulations of tracking, ddsim may be appropriate. Generally for full detector event simulations, use npsim.

    We can check the available flags and options with

    BASH 

    npsim -h

    there’s lots of options! We’ll narrow down to a few:

    • --compactFile
      • Very important, this specifies which geometry definition we will simulate with
      • Try ls $DETECTOR_PATH to see the list of available .xml configurations
    • --numberOfEvents
      • The number of events to process. We’ll keep this low to save time.
    • --inputFiles
      • The file path for the input .hepmc file (or files)
    • --outputFile
      • The file path to output to
    • vX
      • The verbosity level of the output to screen. X is a number between 1 and 7 corresponding to VERBOSE,DEBUG,INFO,WARNING,ERROR,FATAL,ALWAYS
      • E.g. -v5 would select ERROR - We’ll print errors.

    We will try running a short simulation on the events we generated earlier:

    BASH 

    npsim --compactFile $DETECTOR_PATH/epic_craterlake_9x130.xml --numberOfEvents 10 --inputFiles Input.hepmc --outputFile Test_10_Events.edm4hep.root

    This should start running, there’ll be a large info dump to screen with various configuration info loading in. It should not take too long to process.

    Once it’s done, let’s have a quick look at the file.

    Callout

    Time Saving

    For our next step, we’ll want a larger file, I suggest opening a new terminal tab/window and running this simulation in the background as we look at the output we have so far.

    BASH 

    npsim --compactFile $DETECTOR_PATH/epic_craterlake_9x130.xml --numberOfEvents 1000 --inputFiles Input.hepmc --outputFile 1000_Events.edm4hep.root

    We can open it and have a look with ROOT. I recommend you **exit eic-shell and look at the file in root externally if you can. If you don’t have ROOT installed locally, you can use the webviewer, but be aware that it is more limited.

    BASH 

    root Test_10_Events.edm4hep.root

    Within the events tree, we can see a large range of collections. These are primarily collections of hits or contributions to various detector subsystems. For example, the EcalBarrelSciFiHits collection. This collection contains information on the energy and position, as well as cellID of various hits for this detector subsystem. There’s also contributions_begin and contributions_end items which can be used to trace back the individual contributions to a given hit.

    If you check other Hits type collections, you’ll see very similar content. Some may have more or less info. Also of interest is the MCParticles collection. This contains the original MC information from our input file. This is retained so we can always check the actual input for a given event.

    For analysis purposes, we may want this information to study the response of a particular detector in a lot of detail, or perhaps to develop a new reconstruction algorithm. Generally though, this information isn’t particularly useful if we want to do a physics analysis. We need to reconstruct our events first. We’ll do this in the next part of our lesson.

    Callout

    The Afterburner

    We processed our simulation output “as is”. In doing so, we’ve ignored the impact of beam effects on our initial and final state particles. We could add these effects in using the afterburner. This piece of software adds in a large combination of effects to our MC file, including the beam crossing angle, beam divergences and crab cavity impacts. The overall effect is to slightly alter components of the beam and final state particle momentum. For realistic physics simulations, we should generally apply the afterburner. Doing so is simple, within eic-shell we can simply run:

    BASH 

    abconv -p <<preset>> <<Input_File>> -o <<Output_File>>

    where <<preset>> is the beam configuration preset to use and <<Output_File>> is the output file to write to (do not include a file suffix). Other options and flags are available, as usual, try abconv -h.

    Note that the afterburner will try to automatically detect the beam configuration if the -p option is not used. Available presets can be seen from the output of abconv -h, but some are not printed by default. See Lines 2110-2166 for the fill list of configurations available.

    Key Points
    • Before running the simulations in eic-shell, we need to load in a detector config
    • npsim should be used for simulations generally
    • Simulations can take some time to run
    • The output is largely cell/element level hit distributions
    • MC truth info is retained in the simulation output
    • When simulating physics events, we should afterburn our input first

    Content from Reconstructing our Simulated Output

    Last updated on 2026-11-06 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 30 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is EICrecon?
    • What does EICrecon do?
    • How do we process events through EICrecon?

    Objectives

    • Process our simulated events through EICrecon

    Introduction

    As mentioned at the end of the last page, our simulation output itself isn’t really that useful for physics analysis. We need to reconstruct our events first. In doing so, we will reconstruct things like tracks and clusters from our raw detector hit information. We can then assign these to particles for example.

    The ePIC software that does this step for us is called EICrecon. EICrecon is a JANA based reconstruction for the ePIC detector. We can process our simulation output through EICrecon to get reconstructed events that we can then analyse and interpret. As before, we’ll see how we can run EICrecon and some common flags, then we’ll process our output in full as we look at the sample output from a quick run.

    Running EICrecon

    As with our simulation, EICrecon is installed within eic-shell. We can check the available options and flags via:

    BASH 

    eicrecon -h

    Again, when we run, we’ll want to provide a few of these flags, namely:

    • -Ppodio:output_file
      • Specify the file to output to, example usage
        • -Ppodio:output_file=test_output.root
    • -Pjana:nevents
      • The number of events from our input file to run, example usage
        • -Pjana:nevents=100 \(\rightarrow\) run 100 events
    • -Pdd4hep:xml_files
      • The detector configuration file that was used in the simulation and to base our reconstruction on. Example usage
        • -Pdd4hep:xml_files=epic_craterlake.xml
        • Note that by default, EICrecon will search for this file in $DECTOR_PATH, so we need to source our detector geometry before running EICrecon still

    Our input file is specified as an argument without a flag. So as an example command to run our 10 event file from before, we would run:

    BASH 

    eicrecon -Ppodio:output_file=Test_10_Events_Reco.root -Pjana:nevents=1000 -Pdd4hep:xml_files=epic_craterlake_9x130.xml Test_10_Events.edm4hep.root

    again, once we run this, we’ll get some configuration info dumped to screen and then it should run relatively quickly.

    Let’s look at the output

    Callout

    Time Saving (Again)

    As before, due to how long the reconstruction will take, I recommend running a longer reconstruction in the background as we look at our small initial file.

    BASH 

    eicrecon -Ppodio:output_file=1000_Events_Reco.root -Pjana:nevents=10 -Pdd4hep:xml_files=epic_craterlake_9x130.xml 1000_Events.edm4hep.root

    EICrecon Output File

    Our output file now contains quite a few more collections. Again, many of these connect directly to specific detectors. Now though, these collections relate to reconstructed quantities such as calorimeter clusters or particle tracks. For example, B0ECalClusters, is a collection of information tied to clusters in the B0 Electromagnetic Calorimeter. We also have hit level information in some collections.

    There are two new sets of collections we need to take closer look at though. We now have collections with Associations involved somewhere in the name. These collections exist to help us map between reconstructed info and simulated (i.e. MC truth) information. For simulated data, we can know which MC truth particle caused a particular track or cluster and map between the two. This is useful for understanding what has actually happened in our event and we will explore it further in the next part of our tutorial. However, note that for real experimental data, we cannot map between the truth and the reconstruction in this way. So we need to be careful when using this power, particularly if we try to make selections of data using this information.

    The other new type of collection is Reconstructed particles or jets. These collections group together reconstructed detector information (tracks, clusters, PID etc) and present to us a set of candidates for each of our events. For example ReconstructedParticles is a collection of particles that EICrecon has constructed based upon the detector reconstruction in the central detector. Looking at this collection, we see info we could use to construct 4-vectors for particles in our event.

    We can take a quick look at this information directly from the file with TTree->Draw() style commands. Open the file with:

    BASH 

    root Test_10_Events_Reco.root

    Opening Output Files

    Remember to open and inspect the resulting ROOT output files in a local terminal environment outside of eic-shell. Interactive ROOT graphics and TBrowser windows typically require a local display environment to render properly.

    then we can use:

    C++ 

    events->Draw("ReconstructedParticles.QUANTITY")

    to draw a quantity we want (e.g. try putting energy in place of QUANTITY . By default, ROOT will automatically draw this to a 1D histogram with 100 bins. These 100 bins will span the full range of available data. This is often not that useful. We can instead define a histogram ourselves to draw our selection to:

    C++ 

    events->Draw("ReconstructedParticles.QUANTITY>>h1(NBins, xLow, xHigh)")

    will define a new histogram, h1 with NBins between xLow and xHigh. Most importantly, we can actually define and impose some selection cuts on the events we draw too. This does not have to be on the quantity we’re drawing. For example, we could draw our quantity only for charged particles with:

    C++ 

    events->Draw("ReconstructedParticles.QUANTITY>>h1(NBins, xLow, xHigh)", "ReconstructedParticles.charge!=0")

    Finally, we could also even provide some draw options:

    C++ 

    events->Draw("ReconstructedParticles.QUANTITY>>h1(NBins, xLow, xHigh)", "ReconstructedParticles.charge!=0", "HISTERR")

    where HISTERR will draw our histogram as a histogram with error bars.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Quick TTree->Draw() Analysis

    From your file, draw a histogram of \(P_{z}\) for Recosntructed Particles that have an energy under 20 GeV and are negatively charged.

    Draw this histogram with error bars. Configure your number of bins and bin width appropriately (with 10 events this won’t really matter, for 1000, it should start to matter a bit more).

    Key Points
